# How users adjust trust in automation: Contrast effect and hindsight bias

X. Jessie Yang<sup>1</sup>, Christopher D. Wickens<sup>2,3</sup>, Katja Hölttä-Otto<sup>4</sup>

1. Department of Industrial and Operations Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 2. Alion Science & Technology, Boulder, CO 3. Department of Psychology, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO 4. [Department of Mechanical](http://edp.tkk.fi/en/) Engineering, Aalto University, Espoo, Finland

The present study examined how users adjusted their trust towards an automated decision aid. Results revealed that a valid recommendation of the decision aid increases whereas an invalid one reduces trust in automation. The magnitude of trust decrement is greater than that of trust increment. More importantly, this study showed that trust adjustment is not benchmarked strictly against predetermined objective criteria, that is, the decision aid’s recommendation quality. Rather, users’ ability of performing a task themselves and final task outcomes moderate the effects of recommendation quality. A valid recommendation is less appreciated if users are more capable of completing a task by themselves. An invalid recommendation is less penalized if the final task performance is not harmed, as if the invalid recommendation is “forgiven” to a certain degree.

## INTRODUCTION

## Consider the following hypothetical situation:

Patients A and B had exactly the same medical condition and their doctor had to decide whether both patients were at risk of colorectal cancer and if follow-up colonoscopy examinations were necessary. A clinical decision support system suggested that both patients had very low possibility of getting colorectal cancer and colonoscopy examinations were unnecessary. Their doctor agreed with the prognosis.

Patient A, fully covered by insurance, still requested a follow-up colonoscopy examination, which revealed cancerous polyps in his colon. A polypectomy afterwards removed those polyps and saved his life. In contrast, Patient B, constrained by his financial status, decided not to proceed with a colonoscopy. Soon after that, unfortunately, he was diagnosed with colonoscopy cancer.

For both patients, the clinical decision support system made a wrong diagnosis, therefore we would expect a decrement of trust towards the system in both cases, but would the levels of decrement equal to each other? Probably not, as we show in the current research.

Past research has shown that users calibrate their trust in automation based on the experience they have using automated technologies (Lee & See, 2004; Manzey, Reichenbach, & Onnasch, 2012; Merritt & Illgen, 2008; Seong & Bisantz, 2008). It was proposed that there are two feedback loops in the calibration process, namely a positive feedback loop and a negative feedback loop (Manzey et al., 2012). The positive feedback loop is triggered by the experience of automation success, and the negative feedback loop is

activated by the experience of automation failures. In addition, the negative feedback loop engenders a much stronger influence on trust adjustment than the positive feedback loop (Manzey et al., 2012).

In this paper, we aimed to (1) provide empirical evidence on how positive and negative experiences with automation affect trust adjustment, (2) investigate other factors that may influence trust adjustment, specifically, of interest were the moderating effects of contrast effect (Schwarz, Mnnkel, & Hippler, 1990) and hindsight bias (Fischhoff, 1977).

Contrast effects refer to the tendency of decision makers to evaluate an individual/event by benchmarking them against another individual/event, rather than against predetermined objective criteria (Schwarz, Mnnkel, & Hippler, 1990). This effect has been well-documented in research of perception and decision making. In a study of interviewers’ evaluations of job applicants, Wexley, Yukl, Kovacs, and Sanders (1972) found that the evaluation of an average applicant degrades if his or her immediately preceding applicant is highly suitable for a position, whereas upgrades if the immediately preceding applicant is less suitable. Similar effects have been reported in judgment of physical attractiveness (Kenrick & Gutierres, 1980), judgment of products and service (Lynch & Mitra, 1991) and facial identity perception (Hsu & Lee, 2016). In the context of trust in automation, we speculated that an automated technology is evaluated by benchmarking its performance against how a user is able to perform a task by him- or her-self. An automated technology will be evaluated more favorably if the user is less capable of completing the task on his or her own and vice versa.

The hindsight bias refers to the tendency of decision makers to determine the quality of a decision on the basis of the event outcome (Fischhoff, 1977), and it has been documented in medical diagnosis (Arkes, Faust, Guilmette, &

Hart, 1988), court judgement (Starr & McCormick, 2001), accounting and auditing decisions (Peecher & Piercey, 2008) and many other contexts. We postulated that hindsight bias plays a role in trust adjustment in automation, in the sense that a valid recommendation will be less appreciated if the final outcome is negative and an invalid recommendation will be less penalized if the final outcome is positive.

In the present study, we tested the following hypotheses:

**H1a**: Trust in automation will increase when automation makes a valid recommendation and decrease when automation makes an invalid recommendation.

**H1b**: The magnitude of trust decrement will be greater than that of trust increment.

**H2a**: A valid automation recommendation will lead to greater increment of trust, if a user is less capable of completing the task on his or her own and vice versa.

**H2b**: An invalid automation recommendation will lead to greater decrement of trust, if a user is more capable of completing the task on his or her own and vice versa.

**H3a**: A valid automation recommendation will lead to less increment of trust, if the final outcome of a task is undesirable and vice versa.

**H3b**: An invalid automation recommendation will lead to less decrement of trust, if the final outcome of a task is desirable and vice versa.

We examined these hypotheses in an experiment where a participant performed a two alternative forced choice (2AFC) recognition manually, subsequently received imperfect advice from a decision aid, and then performed a final recognition. Based on the accuracy of the participant’s initial recognition, the decision aid’s recommendation and the accuracy of the participant’s final recognition, we could identify eight patterns posteriorly (Table 1). For example, pattern 3 (3 in decimal number is 011 in binary number) refers to the condition where a participant made a wrong initial recognition choice (0), and after receiving a valid automation recommendation (1), altered his or her initial decision in the final recognition (1). It is important to note that we were unable to directly manipulate a participant’s initial recognition nor his or her final recognition. Therefore, an individual participant did **not necessarily** have data points for all the 8 patterns.

## METHODOLOGY

## Experimental task

The current experiment was built upon the memory recognition task of Tulving (see Tulving, 1981; Yang, Park, Wickens, & Helander, 2014 for details). In step 1, participants viewed a series of 150 pictures consisting of 60 target pictures and 90 buffering items, each for two seconds. After that, as a filler task participants wrote down what they knew about 4 well-known people, in 4 minutes. In step 3, participants perform 40 trials of two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) memory recognition. The first three steps aimed to replicate the memory recognition task in Tulving (1981).

In step 4, the participants were presented with their initial recognition selection and a recommendation from an automated decision aid and were asked to make their final recognition selection (Figure 2). The participants were informed that the recommendation given by the decision aid was imperfect and might or might not be correct.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 1: Flowchart of experimental task

Once the participants made their final recognition selection, they received immediate feedback on their performance. At the end of each recognition trial, participants indicated their trust towards the automated decision aid using a six-point trust scale. The points on the scale were 50%, 60%, 70%, 80%, 90% and 100%, with the leftmost point labeled “I don’t trust it (automation) at all. It’s guessing.” and the right most point “I trust it (automation) absolutely”.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 2: Illustration of step 4

Participants completed a practice session with 12 pictures prior to the actual task.

## Participants

The study was approved by the university institutional review board. 67 undergraduate and graduate students with an average age of 25.1 participated in the experiment. They were either paid 5 dollars or earned course credits for participation.

## Experimental design

**Independent variable** The first independent variable was automation reliability (60%, 70%, 80% 90%), manipulated between-subject, the effects of which are not presented in this paper. The second independent variable is the pattern of recognition performance.

**Dependent variable** The dependent variable is trust adjustment, which is calculated as the difference between the nth and the (n-1)th trial.

Trust adjustment (n) = Trust (n) – Trust (n-1)

## RESULTS

The number of occurrence for each of the eight patterns was calculated a posteriori. Due to the extremely low occurrence rate of patterns 1 and 6, they were excluded from the analysis. In addition, as automation reliability was not of interest in the current study, the data were collapsed across the four levels of automation reliability. Table 2 shows the mean and SE values of trust adjustment, and the **magnitude** of trust adjustment for each of the six patterns.

Due to the exclusion of patterns 1 and 6, it was not appropriate to analyze the data using a 2×2×2 repeated ANOVA. Instead, we conducted a series of planned comparisons to test the six hypotheses.

Table 2: Trust adjustment for the six patterns (| | refers to magnitude)

| P | n | Initial recog. | Recom. | Final recog. | Trust adjust | \| Trust adjust \| |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 63 | Wrong | Wrong | Wrong | -4.0(0.5) | 4.3 (0.4) |
| 4 | 47 | Correct | Wrong | Wrong | -6.2(1.2) | 6.4 (1.2) |
| 5 | 59 | Correct | Wrong | Correct | -4.3(0.6) | 4.3 (0.6) |
| 2 | 67 | Wrong | Correct | Wrong | 2.0 (0.3) | 2.3 (0.3) |
| 3 | 57 | Wrong | Correct | Correct | 2.7 (0.5) | 3.1 (0.5) |
| 7 | 67 | Correct | Correct | Correct | 1.5 (0.2) | 1.6 (0.2) |

Recall in H1a, we hypothesized a trust increment upon a valid automation recommendation and a decrement upon an invalid one. To test this hypothesis, we examined the direction of trust adjustment. Specifically, we examined trust adjustments for patterns 2, 3 and 7, all receiving correct automation recommendations, and tested whether the adjustments are above 0. Similarly, for patterns 0, 4 and 5, all receiving wrong automation recommendations, we tested whether the trust adjustments are below 0. One sample t-tests with Bonferroni adjustment (adjusted α = .017) showed that valid automation recommendations increased trust in

automation (Pattern 2: $t(66)=6.243,p<.001$ ; Pattern 3: t(56) $4.847, p < .001$ ; Pattern 7: $t(66)=7.332,p<.001$ , and invalid automation recommendations led to a decrement of trust (Pattern 0: t(62) = -8.700, p < .001; Pattern 4: t(46) = - 5.151, $p \leq . 0 0 1 ;$ ; Pattern $5 : t(62) = -6.870, p < .001$

In H1b, we hypothesized that the magnitude of trust decrement is stronger than that of trust increment. To examine it, we contrasted pattern 0 (wrong initial recognition-**wrong** recommendation-wrong final recognition) against pattern 2 (wrong initial recognition-**correct** recommendation-wrong final recognition), and we compared pattern 5 (correct initial recognition-**wrong** recommendation-correct final recognition) against pattern 7 (correct initial recognition-**correct** recommendation-correct final recognition). It is important to note that the only differing variable within the two contrast pairs is the decision aid’s recommendation. 2-tailed paired sample t-tests with Bonferroni adjustment (adjusted α = .025) showed significantly higher **magnitude** of downward trust adjustment for pattern 0 (wrong recommendation) compared to the upward adjustment of pattern 2 (correct recommendation) $(t(62) = 4.495, p < .001)$ (Figure 3), and for pattern 5 (wrong recommendation) compared to pattern 7 (correct recommendation) (t(58) = 5.247, p < .001) (Figure 4). The two planned comparisons consistently showed that an invalid automation recommendation, compared to a valid one, entails a stronger effect on trust adjustment.

Figure 3: Comparison of magnitude of trust adjustment between pattern 0 and pattern 2

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 4: Comparison of magnitude of trust adjustment between pattern 5 and pattern 7

To examine H2a, that trust increment due to a valid automation recommendation will be greater if the human operator is less capable of completing the task manually and vice versa, we compared pattern 3 (**wrong** initial recognitioncorrect recommendation-correct final recognition) against

pattern 7 (**correct** initial recognition-correct recommendationcorrect final recognition). The only differing variable in this contrast pair is the human operator’s initial recognition performance. A 2-tailed paired sample t-test showed greater trust increment for pattern 3 (wrong initial recognition) compared to pattern 7 (correct initial recognition) $( t ( 5 6 ) =$ $2 . 3 1 5 , p = . 0 2 4 )$ . This suggests that how well a user can perform a task manually moderates the effects of decision aid’s recommendation quality. The impact of a valid automation recommendation is diminished when the human operator is capable of completing the task manually (Figure 5).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 5: Comparison of trust increment between pattern 3 and pattern 7

In H2b, we posited that trust **decrement** due to an invalid automation recommendation will be greater if a user is more capable of completing the task manually and vice versa. We compared pattern 0 (**wrong** initial recognition-wrong recommendation-wrong final recommendation) against pattern 4 (**correct** initial recognition-wrong recommendation-wrong final recommendation), between which the varying variable is the initial recognition quality. A 2-tailed paired sample t-test showed that the trend was in the expected direction, however the difference did not reach significance level $(t(62) = 1.226, p$ = .227).

H3a hypothesized that trust increment upon a valid recommendation will be larger if the final outcome is positive. To test this hypothesis, we compared pattern 2 (wrong initial recognition-correct recommendation-**wrong** final recognition) against pattern 3 (wrong initial recognition-correct recommendation-**correct** final recognition). The difference between the two patterns is the final recognition performance. A 2-tailed paired sample t-test showed a non-significant difference $(t(56) = -1.409, p = 164)$ , although the result is in the expected direction.

H3b hypothesized that trust decrement upon an invalid recommendation will be reduced if the final outcome is positive. We compared pattern 4 (correct initial recognitionwrong recommendation-**wrong** final recognition) against pattern 5 (correct initial recognition-wrong recommendation**correct** final recognition), between which the varying variable is final recognition performance. A 2-tailed paired sample ttest showed a larger trust decrement for pattern 4 (wrong final recognition) in contrast to pattern 5 (correct final recognition) $(t(39) = -3.826, p < .001)$ . Trust decrement upon an invalid recommendation is diminished given a positive final outcome (Figure 6).

Figure 6: Comparison of trust decrement between Pattern 4 and Pattern 5

## DISCUSSION

Overtrust or undertrust towards imperfect automation could lead to suboptimal decision making and harm task performance (Wickens, Hollands, Banbury, & Parasuraman, 2013). Therefore, it is crucial to understand the underlying mechanism of how human users adjust their trust in automation.

Past research proposed a two-feedback-loops mechanism in trust adjustment, and assumed a stronger effect of the negative feedback loop in contrast to the positive loop (de Vries, Middent, & Bouwhuis, 2003; Dzindolet, Peterson, Pomranky, Pierce, & Beck, 2003; Lee & Moray, 1992, 1994; Manzey et al., 2012). Consistent with previous studies (Manzey et al., 2012; Yuviler-Gavish & Gopher, 2011), the present study supports **H1a**, showing an average of 2.1% **increment** of trust upon receiving a valid recommendation and an average of 4.8% **decrement** of trust upon receiving an invalid recommendation. Moreover, results from this study provided statistical evidence for the assumption that the negative feedback loop engenders a larger effect than the positive feedback loop (**H1b**) (Figures 3 & 4). Such asymmetric influence could be explained by two reasons. First, it could be due to the human users’ high expectation of an automated technology at the initial stage of interaction (Muir & Moray, 1996). One on hand, valid recommendations are anticipated, which could lead to slow increment of trust. On the other hand, invalid recommendations violate expectations, which could result in dramatic drop of trust. Second, trust adjustment might resemble prospect theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979), in which gain (valid recommendation) is evaluated less positively than loss (invalid recommendation) is evaluated negatively.

More importantly, we proposed that the two-feedbackloops mechanism is moderated by a human user’s ability of completing a task and the final task outcome. We hypothesized that a valid automation recommendation would engender greater trust **increment** if a human operator is less capable (**H2a**) or if the final outcome is desirable (**H3a**), and an invalid automation recommendation would yield greater trust **decremen**t if a human operator is more capable (**H2b**), or if the final outcome is undesirable (**H3b**).

Results from the currently study partially support our hypotheses, that contrast effect and hindsight bias do matter in trust adjustment. Contrast effects have been featured in research of human perception and decision making about an individual/event. We found similar trends in humanautomation interaction, that a decision maker evaluates an automated technology by benchmarking it against his or her own ability, rather than against predetermined objective criteria. Here the user’s initial recognition could be regarded as an “anchor” against which the automation will be evaluated. A valid automation recommendation, after a wrong initial recognition, generates a larger contrast against the “anchor”, and hence engenders larger trust increment.

We found the tendency of users to adjust their trust towards automation on the basis of an event outcome, instead of the objective automation recommendation quality. The trust decrement upon a wrong recommendation is smaller when the final performance is still favorable. It is as if the wrong recommendation is “forgiven” to a certain degree, given that it does not harm the final performance.

## CONCLUSION

How to facilitate appropriate trust-reliability calibration is a major research question that scientists studying human-robot interaction and human factors strive to answer (Hoff & Bashir, 2015; Schaefer, Chen, Szalma & Hancock, 2015; Wickens, Clegg, Vieane, & Sebok, 2015). It is, therefore important to understand the nuances and various factors that may influence this critical variable and, as we have done here, understand the dynamics of trust adjustment, as with some of the original models of trust (Lee & Moray, 1994).

In the present study, we examined the effects of a decision aids’ recommendation quality on trust adjustment and how trust adjustment is moderated by the users’ ability of performing a task on his or her own, and the humanautomation team’s final task performance. Our results confirmed the assumption that the negative feedback loop exerted a stronger effect on trust adjustment. More importantly, this study showed that trust adjustment is not benchmarked strictly against predetermined objective criteria, that is, the decision aid’s recommendation quality. Rather, users’ ability of performing a task themselves and final task outcomes moderate the effects of recommendation quality. A valid recommendation is less appreciated if users are more capable of completing a task by themselves. An invalid recommendation is less penalized if the final task performance is not harmed.
